notes.title: Kanda Sashti Vizha Day 9
body: This evening was a mad dash between three temples. Vedapuriswara was to have an unjal utsavam following their Sashti marking. We got there too early (it hadn’t started yet, caught a glimpse of the utsavars still behind curtains) and then too late (it had been over in a blink, staged just near the alankara mandapam in the rear prakaram). Temple was closing by 9 when we reached, all done. Clearly, it had been a smaller-than-usual affair.

Lawspet Murugan was snazzily done up, in contrast. Archways all over with artificial flowers, the sort of backdrops one sees at some wedding receptions and the like. I’m sure it was cheaper to have the decorations done this way, but the shift in aesthetics from the temple’s typical ritual style to this is plain jarring. We’ve not yet in India found a happy aesthetic medium or that price sweet spot that keeps things natural and well-crafted but not ridiculously priced. Folks like Vizha Medai should really look to capture such ground with innovative approaches to floral decoration, the use of common leaves and such. Anyway, there was a dance stage set up on one side, so a bharatanatyam performance was about to begin after the unjal puja.

We spoke to Ramanan Gurukkal briefly, congratulating him on the dancing during the Thirukalyanam which had been genuinely enjoyable good fun. He told us that Koothu Paatu (Tamil koothu music) and Magudi Paatu (with the instruments/mimicking the instruments used by snake charmers) are common at wedding events here. Must be a community specific thing.

He also told us about Paalikai mulaippu, which I realised later is nothing but the Sanskrit Ankurarpanam, or sowing of the nava-danyam at the start of major pujas as a sign of fertility and (as Manish may prefer to say) fecundity, mangalyam. Apparently this temple’s Churnotsavam (happens on the same day as the dhvajavarohanam, the day immediately after soora samharam) involves taking some of these sprouts, pounding them in an ural with turmeric and oil, and applying this to the forehead of the moola murti. Aside from taking the sprouts to the ocean for theerthavari, this is the only variant to the conclusion of the puja cycle that starts with the sowing that we have heard about.

notes.title: Wait, Not Such Lonely Trails After All
body: Ghousiga’s Murugan was out on the streets when we reached, on a vahana meant to be Ravana but without the 10 heads. We found out later that the ten-headed Ravana vahana was swapped out because it was too large to carry on shoulders. It was being carried by a group that included Farhaan and several others we have seen often. Apparently they were all there, and free, so they decided to do this. A trio of drummers accompanied them along with the nadaswaram players, making some rather unique rhythmic sounds and engaging music. They took a shorter route than usual (maybe the one used when they carry only thol-oda? ie. on skin/shoulders), But it was interesting, reassuring even to see a temple that otherwise seemed quite fixated on performance to just move in this spontaneous way, with no dancing nor any audience to speak of save those of us on the streets. Murugan inspired it, perhaps.

At the corner of Bussy and MG Road, they paused for longer. Many people stop to give the men water, soft drinks and anything to sustain them. A flower seller threw handfuls of flowers. After a time, we asked if he’d do it again so we could photograph–and we were surprised by the readiness with which he obliged. Apparently he does this for all the deities that come this way, including the Christian processions, though he is himself staunchly Hindu. Kaliya-Perumal, is his name. He grabbed a large basket of flowers, practically ran to catch up with the procession (which had started moving again) and then took as much delight in tossing them for Murugan as we did taking those photos. He didn’t ask for money for the flowers. Told us instead of his many children and 11 grandchildren, all thriving. Flower selling is his pastime for extra money, is all, he said. I paid him anyway.
What people we meet, in all these ordinary encounters. What people gather because of the temples, what spills out of the temples when the deities emerge. It’s all endlessly moving.

notes.title: Sashti by the Sea
body: Well, it’s the 10th day but Ghousiga’s Sashti celebrations conclude with the Dhvajavarohanam and Kadal Theerthavari. 830am, morning abhishekam to the moolavar was going on. This is dinapadi, a daily affair. Samhara murti was alongside, as was the astra murti.

The makeshift yagasala was cleared. Kalasas taken to the main shrine with the thirai closed, for the final parts of the abhishekam. The happily growing sprouts, koorcham, various pavitrams etc. and the remnants of the last (still smoking) homa kundam were overturned and collected in a bag. The yagasala was returned to being a palliyarai.

The pradhana murti as one priest had told us, is always the one readied for the morning purappadu the night before – he was behind a screen. I suppose alankaram had happened earlier in the morning, and he was in tiger skin, oddly seeming to be out of proportion until we noticed a tail (!) which made this a puli (tiger) alankaram and very endearing. When the second puja was done here, he was moved along with Vinayaka and Veerabahu to the right of the kodi maram, from where he could watch the avarohanam. That started with the usual ubhayakara sankalpam, prayers to Vigneswara, and then proceeded to remove the kaapu threads tied around all those who had given themselves to the Sashti Vizha, human and animate–the kodi maram itself, the maha bali peetham, Murugan’s peacock, all the ashtadigbalis or 8 surrounding bali peethams, the utsavars themselves, and finally the people who had been the festival’s stalwarts, men and some women, too. Following this, the utsavar was lifted and carried around the temple and out (stops at Moolavar and Thulasi Mariamman as always), and seated on the waiting vandi outside. Vinayaka, Veerabahu, Astra murti followed. We did, too. The thattu vandi was loaded with all the kadal-side abhishekam would need, missing nothing, including prasadam. Small aradhanai happened, coconut went PHAT, and the group set off for the Gandhi thidal on the beachfront promenade.

It’s always so surreal to see these deities carried to the beach which is such a modern environment these days, inviting the curiosities of tourists and other passers-by, interrupting the celebratory remnants of a French colonial and military presence which still appear like clusters of barnacles. This is a very different sort of spilling out here than what happens in the markets where the gods passing is a normal event and everyone knows how to receive them and what to do. Here, they are a curiosity. A black Gandhi on one side, a white Nehru on the other, abhishekam to the astra deva happened here, and the Thulasi Mariamman priest (who had changed from the usual veshti to “beach attire,” in the form of a different waist cloth) carried the murti to the ocean. Khadir Sir was there of course (he’s so very hands on, monitoring and guiding literally everything), as was Rajesh Gurukkal.

It seemed like the group had fun in the water. The man carrying the yagasala and sprout remnants emptied them all into the water and washed them away. I saw flowers floating for a while after. The men stayed longer than most theerthavaris we’ve seen, appearing to wait on waves to really come and cover the priest holding the astra murti. The sea was rough, that might have happened in course, but soon they headed back. Rajesh Gurukkal took the astrar, did a quick alankaram, and puja. Pongal and a very coconuty panchamrutam (best I’ve had in long) were handed out as naivedyam.

Tomorrow is the theppotsavam, come for it, was Khadir Sir’s invitation. They will carry Murugan on skin to the Sivan Koyil kulam at 7pm (6, he said, but it will become 7) where this god of love and war will float and frolic on those waters while we come to watch, of course we will.

Note the photos in this set from the temple foyer, which describe a sweating samhara murti. The legend of Murugan sweating முத்து முத்தாக/ beads of sweat like pearls lives on, like all the droplets of seawater that splashed over him today.

notes.title: Preparation for Tomorrow’s Celebrations
body: This evening, the preparatory pujas for Kannika Parameswari’s annual celebrations start. It’s their 11th year, a Kumbhabhishekam is due, everyone says. There are a few ladies around, but the focus of activity is on the ubhayakara and his wife (he’s a Perumal bhakta, someone says; it’s true we’ve often seen him there). The kalasas are out on a stand facing west, and in front of them the usual thonais representing the navagrahas. The priest is reading a namavali, and the couple are jointly putting flowers on the kalasas. They switch eventually to the conches, circling the 108 slowly: she places flowers, he pours water with the panchapatra udharini slowly, I suppose ceremonially (the conches had already been prepped with water, flowers etc.). He had a koorcham bunch in his hands, too. (The conches are set up on a table outside the main sannadhi, and beneath them are three new calendars for 2027). The puja continues, seated, and then circumambulating the kalasas. Homa kundam has been set up for tomorrow’s use, the largest and tallest we’ve seen yet.

Several ladies there are passing by on their way to see Ghousiga’s theppal event. I feel rather happy to have access to live updates from Arun, and to be able to tell them exactly when the purappadu has left and when it might reach the Sivan koyil next door!

notes.title: Afloat on Siva’s Waters
body: The thavil player stands up and prepares to sound the curtain-opening of the alankara mandapa. Beneath him lies a fluttering bunch of paper. “Om Saravana Bhava, Om Saravana Bhava, Om Saravana Bhava…” it reads over and over, page after page, invoking He who is born in the reed-filled waters. A rather fitting invocation because today Murugan journeys from his abode to the waters of Vedapuriswara’s kulam for the theppotsavam float-festival.

The curtains open with the surging thavil-nadaswaram sounds and reveal Subramania’s regal alankaram. He sits cross-legged dressed in white and gold, wearing a large flower-crown, and decked with a massive ixora-chrysanthemum garland. The priest ends his sanskrit chants with “Maharajaya Namah”, and declares this strikingly princely figure to be the monarch of the region. In quick succession, He is lifted on shoulders, taken round the prakara, placed on the vehicle, and pulled out and up the road towards the Vedapuriswara temple by the trusted Ghousiga tractor. We were told yesterday that the procession from Ghousiga to Vedapuriswara would be on shoulder and foot, but perhaps this was changed due to delays. It is already 5 minutes to 8pm, and the tractor jostles its way through the MG road traffic. I got some pictures from the front as it crossed Bussy street, but for the rest of the trip I simply could not get ahead of the tractor!! Murugan’s hurry to meet his Lord must have been pressing. Very quickly the procession arrived at Vedapuriswara and Murugan snugly fit himself just outside the gopuram gateway, looking straight into the sanctum. A series of firecrackers announced this arrival, and the charming Arasu Mama of Vedapuriswara came forward with a kalasa from Siva’s sanctum. This kalasa was briefly held out before Murugan. Who was invoked into this kalasa? Siva himself presumably – and if so, what fascinating symbolic gesture could this be? Kartikeya is born of Siva’s very essence. Perhaps the interaction with the kalasa highlights this? This kalasa is then taken straight back into the sanctum.

An aradhanai follows, and then, dancing and swaying, Ghousiga Balasubramania walks through the gopuram gateway and emerges into the temple space. Quite quickly the procession makes its way to the kulam, where the theppal waits floating. The area of the temple tank has been amply decorated with LED strips highlighting ‘Kausika’ and Murugan’s presence. Coincidentally, the tank itself was cleaned out a few days ago, as though in anticipation of this – though perhaps Murugan would have liked some reeds in his theppal waters! Ghousiga’s own kalasa climbs the theppal first, is worshipped, and its water is sprinkled all around. Murugan is hauled onto it, followed by another aradhanai, and finally – float!
The theppal floats along the periphery carrying temple executives, priests, ubhayakaras, and eventually devotees over its nine rounds.

notes.title: Closing of the Vedapuriswara’s Kanda Sashti Vizha
body: It feels incidental in the face of Ghousiga’s big event, but the Murugan trio at Vedapuriswara also had an alankaram and deeparadhanai this evening–the final puja of this temple’s Sashti festival. They were all put away in their alankara chamber when I (Deepa) saw them, but I did catch some photos to record that this final puja had happened.

notes.title: Homams Taller and Broader
body: It is the second and principal day of Kannika Parameswari’s Aandu Vizha. The morning begins at 530 with a Gopuja. Deepa gets there by 615 (just in time to have the hot paal-naivedyam from the milked cow, whose calf was now suckling rather vigorously), and Arun is still in bed sleeping through his alarm! Deepa catches the tail end of the Gopuja, after which unfolds the long array of homams. The sequence is: Vedaparayanam, Ganapati homam, Aalaya Parivara Devata homam, Sri Kannika Parameswari Gayatri homam, Moolamantra homam, Sri Lalitasahasranama homam, Sri Parvati Svayamvara homam, Santanagopala homam, Dhanvantiri homam, Purnahuti homam. Among all our temple visits, this is the broadest variety of homams we have seen being done together. And to add to this, it is also the tallest homa-kundam, or fire-altar, we have ever seen!

The priest sits to one of its sides, facing the sanctum, offering naivedyam into the fire. To his left are the ubhayakara couple, with the man offering ghee-oblations with the priest’s chants. To his right is the temple nirvagam head, offering oblations of diverse dravyams or substances as per the particular homam’s requirements. Just beyond the fire-altar towards the sanctum are five kalasams placed at a height. Below and in front, west of the kalasas, are the Navagraha thonnais, also on a short stool. And below even this, is a little manjal Vinayaka with an assortment of thonnais. Beyond even the kalasas is a table with the shankhas ready for the subsequent shankhabhishekam. Resting against this table, facing the kalasas, are three new calendars for 2027.

The homams begin by 7am with many of the regular Kannika ladies present. The homa-kundam is 5 bricks tall and 3.5 bricks wide, and its surface holds fruits for the 8 directions. The chants accompanying the homams themselves seem to be much simpler than we have seen elsewhere. The priest repeats one phrase over and over, perhaps 108 times, or perhaps until all of the particular dravyam has been offered. One of the homa-kundam fruits then gets tossed into the fire. We assume this to mark the end of a particular homam. One such series of chants was the repetition of “tat purushaya vidmahe, mahadevaya dheemahi, tanno shanmukha prachodayat”. The Mahamrityunjaya mantra was also done. There was some confusion at one stage about which homam was to be done next, and the printed patrikai had to be called upon for answers. We could not really understand what was decided or resolved. The fruit-tossing which seemed to us to mark the transition between homams also became inconsistent, and we eventually lost track of where in the sequence we were.

The lotus-lily baskets soon made their way to the ubhayakara, who dipped them one by one in a bowl of honey and offered them to Agni. After this there was a moment of major reshuffling in the crowd who repositioned themselves in a semi-circle-like formation, creating a chain from one side of the fire to another. This chain passed on the mooligai (medicinal) dravyams from the nirvagam head to the ubhayakara who offered them. This was followed by the concluding purnahuti and aradhanai, after which the crowd was asked to walk around the entire setup, tossing flowers onto the kalasams every time they passed in front of it. The ubhayakara family were the last to offer some flowers after spinning around on-spot three times.

There was a significant break here, and everybody from the priest to the watchman came together for ven-pongal prasadam. Another hour passed in abhishekam preparations, followed by the abhishekam itself. Then finally came the shankhabhishekam with devotees walking up in a single file. They were handed one shankha each, which they took to the first step of the sanctum and handed to the priest for the abhishekam. Everybody is allowed to hand their conches and join the queue again for another round.
The alankaram would have come after this, followed by a deeparadhanai around noon. But we are unable to make it for these.

notes.title: Preparations for Karthikai Somavaram Shankhabhishekam
body: It’s not Monday yet, but the preparatory homam for tomorrow’s Shankhabhishekam starts the evening before. 4 groups of 10 trays each, each one holding 5 rows of 5 conches each – 250 in each corner, 1000 total, all surround an altar with the main kalasas. They are ordered in 4-2-3-1 “triangles” with the numbers indicating the number of boxes containing 25 shankhas each. We wonder where the remaining 8 of the 1008 are, and are told they are inside some of the main kalasas.

Arasoo mama is officiating, but a few priests have been called in from outside as well. The ubhayakaras as it turns out are a husband and wife who are the heads of the Kanchi Kamakoti Peetham pathashala branch in Pondicherry–they run a goshala, perform weddings for the poor and train priests (the wife is the same one who sponsored the gopujas during Navaratri, and who does the Lalita trishati archanais daily; Ganeshan Meenakshi and family are the officially listed ubhayakaras). Some of their group are here today, chanting. Starts with just the two regular young priests (one of whom is Naresh), and then expands to 7.

They go through rounds of Sri Rudram, at multiple speeds or so it feels. Then Purusha suktam and what must be the Pancha Suktam (because I know we hear the Narayana Suktam and the Durga suktam), Bhagya suktam. They take a break and then come back later as the homam 1st kaalam is beginning, and at that point also chant what sound like the Nakshatra sutram and the Nakshatra Ishti (offerings) from the Taittiriya Brahmana of the Krishna Yajurveda.
Naivedyam is offered to all four sets of 250 shankhas, I notice. And a lamp during deeparadhanai is offered to Agni, which is interesting. What does it mean to offer a lamp to a fire?
